content: Patients with sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) typically appear normal upon physical examination. In approximately 50% of cases, the physical examination findings are entirely unremarkable. During the physical examination of SIDS patients, physicians must carefully assess for any signs of external airway obstruction, head entrapment, or other environmental risk factors that could contribute to the condition. Appearance of the Patient Patients with SIDS generally appear normal. Vital Signs High-grade or low-grade fever may be present in 25% of SIDS cases. Evidence of infection may also be observed in 25% of cases. Physicians should look for any signs of choking or gasping in the infant. Skin Apparent life-threatening events (ALTEs) are often associated with episodes of apnea and changes in skin color. Cyanosis is observed in 50-60% of cases. Pallor and erythema may also be present. Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, and Throat (HEENT) Some patients may exhibit feeding difficulties. Evidence of trauma should be carefully evaluated. Neck The neck examination is usually normal in SIDS patients. However, physicians should check for any signs of obstruction. Lungs Breathing difficulties may be present in 50% of cases. Any signs of respiratory infections should be thoroughly evaluated. Physicians must assess for any obstruction of the external airway. Heart Cardiovascular examination findings may vary and should be carefully evaluated for: Signs of valvular disease. Arrhythmias. Cardiomyopathy. Abdomen The abdominal examination is typically normal in SIDS patients. Back The back examination is usually normal in SIDS patients. Genitourinary The genitourinary examination is generally normal in SIDS patients.
